summary: Full-extraction pass over 20 DOJ False Claims Act documents: the annual FCA recovery press releases FY2007-FY2025 and the Fraud Statistics overview to FY2023. Added the reward-share rule as restated each year, category, state-Medicaid and since-January-2009 totals, settlement counts, 17 qui tam cases named with a whistleblower link, one event, and every remaining cell of the four FY1987-FY2023 statistics tables (1,432 rows; the table adds up within $1-3 rounding). Named settlements that the releases do not link to a qui tam suit or relator are listed in contains, not recorded.

program_rules.notes: Restated in the DOJ annual FCA release; valid dates not given in the release.

cases.summary: Illegal drug pricing and marketing (inflated prices and "spread" marketing, kickbacks to doctors, wholesalers and pharmacies, off-label promotion of Abilify, false best prices for Serzone); civil settlement arising from seven qui tam actions. BMS and Apothecon also paid $187 million to state Medicaid programs.
cases.location: Fact sheet: significant recoveries in fiscal year 2007, BMS item
cases.quote: The six relators will share a $52 million award plus additional amounts from the states.
cases.notes: Award is the federal share shared by six relators; they also get unstated amounts from the states. Sanctions = federal recovery only. Settled in FY2007 (Oct 2006-Sep 2007) according to DOJ's FY2007 fact sheet; exact date not given (in the original release linked there).

cases.summary: Inflated reported prices for the drug Anzemet and marketing of the spread; Aventis also paid $10 million to several states.
cases.location: Fact sheet: significant recoveries in fiscal year 2007, Aventis item
cases.quote: The relators shared a $33 million award.
cases.notes: Award shared by the relators. Settled in FY2007 (Oct 2006-Sep 2007) according to DOJ's FY2007 fact sheet; exact date not given (in the original release linked there).

cases.summary: False claims in the FEHBP mail-order drug benefit (cancelled prescriptions, shorted pills, billing for services not provided) and kickbacks; settlement resolved two qui tam lawsuits and a separate federal investigation.
cases.location: Fact sheet: significant recoveries in fiscal year 2007, Medco item
cases.quote: The relators received $23.9 million as their award.
cases.notes: Sanctions cover both qui tam suits and the separate investigation. Settled in FY2007 (Oct 2006-Sep 2007) according to DOJ's FY2007 fact sheet; exact date not given (in the original release linked there).

cases.summary: Defective pricing disclosures to GSA for PeopleSoft software and maintenance (1997-2005); qui tam by a former PeopleSoft employee; record GSA fraud settlement.
cases.location: Fact sheet: significant recoveries in fiscal year 2007, Oracle item
cases.quote: The relator received $17.7 million as his statutory award.
cases.notes: Settled in FY2007 (Oct 2006-Sep 2007) according to DOJ's FY2007 fact sheet; exact date not given (in the original release linked there).

cases.target: Harbert International, Inc. and related Harbert companies
cases.summary: Judgment after a seven-week trial for conspiracy to rig bids on USAID-financed wastewater treatment contracts in Cairo, Egypt; damages of $34 million trebled plus $10,000 penalties on 111 claims, reduced by earlier co-conspirator settlements.
cases.location: Fact sheet: significant recoveries in fiscal year 2007, Harbert item
cases.quote: $90 million judgment after trial against Harbert International, Inc.
cases.notes: Judgment, not a settlement; the fact sheet says the relator's award has yet to be determined (so a qui tam case). Other defendants also liable for portions (Harbert Construction Services (U.K.) Ltd. and an individual). Judgment in FY2007 (Oct 2006-Sep 2007) according to DOJ's FY2007 fact sheet; exact date not given (in the original release linked there).

cases.summary: Caused the District of Columbia child and family services agency to bill Medicaid for targeted case management for every foster child whether or not services were provided; relator a former Maximus division manager. Maximus also entered a deferred prosecution agreement.
cases.location: Fact sheet: significant recoveries in fiscal year 2007, Maximus item
cases.quote: The relator, a former division manager with Maximus, received $4.93 million as his share of the recovery.
cases.notes: Settled in FY2007 (Oct 2006-Sep 2007) according to DOJ's FY2007 fact sheet; exact date not given (in the original release linked there).

cases.summary: Off-label marketing of Actimmune for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis; InterMune also paid $6.7 million to state Medicaid programs.
cases.location: Fact sheet: significant recoveries in fiscal year 2007, InterMune item
cases.quote: The relator received $5.7 million as her share of the recovery.
cases.notes: Settled in FY2007 (Oct 2006-Sep 2007) according to DOJ's FY2007 fact sheet; exact date not given (in the original release linked there).

cases.target: State of New York and New York City
cases.summary: Record settlement of federal Medicaid claims, triggered by a qui tam suit.
cases.location: press release text, para 8
cases.quote: In a record settlement of federal Medicaid claims, the state of New York and New York City agreed to pay the United States $540 million.
cases.notes: The release says both FY2009 records were "triggered by qui tam suits". Relator share not given. Settled in FY2009 (Oct 2008-Sep 2009); exact date not given.

cases.target: NetApp Inc. and NetApp U.S. Public Sector Inc.
cases.summary: Record General Services Administration defective pricing settlement, triggered by a qui tam suit.
cases.location: press release text, para 8
cases.quote: And in a record settlement in a General Services Administration defective pricing case, NetApp Inc. and NetApp U.S. Public Sector Inc. paid the government $128.7 million.
cases.notes: The release says both FY2009 records were "triggered by qui tam suits". Relator share not given. Settled in FY2009 (Oct 2008-Sep 2009); exact date not given.

cases.summary: The government intervened in a whistleblower suit and filed a complaint alleging CA overcharged for software licences and maintenance under a GSA Multiple Award Schedule contract (incomplete and inaccurate commercial pricing disclosures).
cases.location: "Other Fraud Recoveries and Actions" section, CA Inc. paragraph
cases.quote: The government filed a complaint against global software provider CA Inc. after intervening in a whistleblower suit against the company.
cases.notes: Complaint filed in FY2014 (Oct 2013-Sep 2014); exact date not given; no amount; pending at the time of the release.

cases.summary: Qui tam by a cardiac nurse and a health care reimbursement consultant against hundreds of hospitals implanting cardiac devices in Medicare patients contrary to CMS criteria; DOJ settled with nearly 500 hospitals for $250 million in total, $216 million of it in FY2015.
cases.location: "Health Care Fraud" section, para 3 (hospitals)
cases.quote: The department settled with nearly 500 of these hospitals for a total of $250 million, including $216 million recovered in the past fiscal year.
cases.notes: Many settlements with nearly 500 hospitals counted together as one matter; $216 million recovered in FY2015 (Oct 2014-Sep 2015), the rest earlier or later; dates not given. Relator share not given.

cases.target: Berkeley HeartLab Inc.; BlueWave Healthcare Consultants Inc.; Floyd Calhoun Dent III; Robert Bradley Johnson; LaTonya Mallory
cases.summary: DOJ intervened in three qui tam suits against a cardiovascular testing laboratory, a marketing company, BlueWave's owners and HDL's co-founder and former CEO.
cases.location: "Individual accountability" section, para 2
cases.quote: the department intervened in three qui tam suits against another laboratory, Berkeley HeartLab Inc., a marketing company, BlueWave Healthcare Consultants Inc. and three individuals
cases.notes: Intervention in FY2015 (Oct 2014-Sep 2015); dates not given; "These matters are ongoing." The earlier $48.5 million settlements with Health Diagnostics Laboratory and Singulex are not linked to a qui tam suit in the release, so not recorded as a case. Defendants named by DOJ.

cases.target: Dr. Asad Qamar and the Institute for Cardiovascular Excellence PLLC
cases.summary: DOJ intervened in two qui tam suits alleging medically unnecessary peripheral artery procedures billed to Medicare and kickbacks to patients by waiving copayments.
cases.location: "Individual accountability" section, para 2
cases.quote: The department also intervened in two qui tam suits against Florida cardiologist Dr. Asad Qamar and his practice, the Institute for Cardiovascular Excellence PLLC
cases.notes: Intervention in FY2015; date not given; ongoing. Defendant named by DOJ.

cases.summary: Kickbacks to clinics and physicians to use a bioengineered skin substitute; the settlement also resolved relators' allegations of off-label marketing, false price statements and improper coding. $343.9 million federal and $6.1 million to state Medicaid.
cases.location: "Health Care Fraud" section, para 2 (Shire)
cases.quote: the settlement also resolved allegations brought by relators that Shire and ABH unlawfully marketed the skin substitute for uses not approved by the FDA
cases.notes: Sanctions = total settlement including $6.1 million to states. Relator share not given. Settled in FY2017 (Oct 2016-Sep 2017); exact date not given.

cases.target: HealthCare Partners Holdings LLC (d/b/a DaVita Medical Holdings LLC)
cases.summary: Inaccurate information causing Medicare Advantage Organizations to receive inflated payments; partly a voluntary disclosure by DaVita, and the settlement also resolved whistleblower allegations of "one-way" chart reviews.
cases.location: "Health Care Fraud" section, HCP paragraph
cases.quote: In addition, this settlement resolved whistleblower allegations that HCP engaged in “one-way” chart reviews
cases.notes: Settlement covers both the self-disclosed conduct and the whistleblower allegations. Relator share not given. Settled in FY2018 (Oct 2017-Sep 2018); exact date not given.

cases.summary: DOJ intervened and filed a complaint in a lawsuit alleging the Medicare Advantage organisation submitted or caused inaccurate diagnosis information to raise Medicare risk-adjustment payments.
cases.location: "Health Care Fraud" section, Medicare Advantage paragraph 2
cases.quote: the department intervened and filed complaints in separate lawsuits against Independent Health Corporation and members of the Kaiser Permanente consortium
cases.notes: Intervention by the government is only possible in a qui tam (relator) suit, so this is treated as a whistleblower case although the release does not use the words qui tam or relator. Intervened in FY2021 (Oct 2020-Sep 2021); exact date not given; no amount; pending.

cases.target: Members of the Kaiser Permanente consortium
cases.summary: DOJ intervened and filed a complaint in a separate lawsuit alleging inaccurate diagnosis information submitted to raise Medicare Advantage risk-adjustment payments.
cases.location: "Health Care Fraud" section, Medicare Advantage paragraph 2 (second suit)
cases.quote: the department intervened and filed complaints in separate lawsuits against Independent Health Corporation and members of the Kaiser Permanente consortium
cases.notes: Intervention by the government is only possible in a qui tam (relator) suit, so this is treated as a whistleblower case although the release does not use the words qui tam or relator. Intervened in FY2021 (Oct 2020-Sep 2021); exact date not given; no amount; pending.

cases.summary: Kickbacks (speaker honoraria, training and consulting fees, meals) to physicians in connection with multiple sclerosis drugs Avonex, Tysabri and Tecfidera, 2009-2014; a case pursued by a whistleblower.
cases.location: "Health Care Fraud" section, kickbacks paragraph 4
cases.quote: In a case pursued by a whistleblower, the pharmaceutical company Biogen Inc. paid $843.8 million to resolve allegations
cases.notes: Relator not named in the release; relator share not given. Resolved in FY2022 (Oct 2021-Sep 2022); exact date not given.

cases.summary: DOJ intervened in a case alleging the Medicare Advantage organisation submitted or failed to correct inaccurate diagnosis information to increase reimbursement.
cases.location: "Health Care Fraud" section, Medicare Advantage paragraph
cases.quote: This past year, the department intervened in one case against Cigna Corp
cases.notes: Intervention by the government is only possible in a qui tam (relator) suit, so treated as a whistleblower case; the release does not use the words qui tam or relator here. FY2022; exact date not given; pending.

cases.target: Two laboratory CEOs, a hospital CEO, six physicians and other individuals and entities (not named in the release)
cases.summary: DOJ intervened in qui tam actions and filed a complaint alleging referrals in violation of the Anti-Kickback Statute and Stark Law and medically unnecessary laboratory testing billed to federal programs.
cases.location: "Health Care Fraud" section, kickbacks paragraph 2
cases.quote: The department intervened and pursued claims under the False Claims Act in several qui tam actions alleging kickback violations.
cases.notes: Example given of the "several qui tam actions" with intervention; defendants not named in the release. FY2022; exact date not given; pending.

cases.summary: DOJ filed a complaint in intervention in a whistleblower lawsuit alleging Rite Aid filled unlawful prescriptions for controlled substances (May 2014-June 2019), in violation of the FCA and the Controlled Substances Act.
cases.location: "Opioids" section, para 2
cases.quote: This year, the Justice Department filed a complaint in intervention in a whistleblower lawsuit against Rite Aid Corporation and various subsidiaries
cases.notes: FY2023 (Oct 2022-Sep 2023); exact date not given; no amount; pending.

events.title: DOJ launches the Civil Cyber-Fraud Initiative
events.description: The Deputy Attorney General announced an initiative to use the False Claims Act against misrepresentations by contractors about cybersecurity of IT, software and cloud services bought by the government.
events.quote: On Oct. 6, 2021, the Deputy Attorney General announced the department’s Civil Cyber-Fraud Initiative to use the False Claims Act to combat new and emerging cyber threats.

new_indicators.name: Settlements and judgments (number)
new_indicators.definition: Number of settlements and judgments a programme obtained in a period (e.g. DOJ False Claims Act settlements and judgments), whistleblower cases or not; breakdown category= for a subset.
new_indicators.notes: proposed by extract-whistleblowing-usa4 (DOJ FCA releases from FY2022 print the number of settlements and judgments; companion to recoveries_total).

gaps: DOJ annual releases name hundreds of FCA settlements without saying whether a whistleblower brought them; by rule they are listed in the ledger contains only, so the cases table under-counts qui tam cases from these releases.

ledger.contains: DOJ press release 07-873 (1 Nov 2007) on FY2007 FCA recoveries: $2 billion total; more than $20 billion since 1986; $1.45 billion from qui tam suits; $177 million to relators; health care $1.54 billion; DoD $48.4 million; relator share rules (15-25%, up to 30%); civil penalty of $5,500-$11,000 per claim (defendants' liability, not a reward rule, not recorded); $264 million returned to state Medicaid in pharmaceutical cases; fact sheet of 11 significant recoveries. Already in the data: 6 observations. Added: 3 rules, the state Medicaid figure and 7 qui tam cases (BMS, Aventis, Medco, Oracle/PeopleSoft, Harbert judgment, Maximus, InterMune). Not cases because the release does not link them to a qui tam suit or relator: Zimmer/Depuy/Biomet/Smith & Nephew $311 million, Amerigroup $172 million judgment, Purdue $100.6 million, Burlington Resources $97.5 million ($105.3 million with interest), Mellon Bank $34.6 million. "More than $800 million" from five named pharmaceutical settlements is a sum of named settlements, not a category total, so not recorded.

DOJ press release 08-992 (10 Nov 2008) on FY2008 FCA recoveries: $1.34 billion total; more than $21 billion since 1986; almost 78% from qui tam suits; $198 million to relators; health care $1.12 billion; defence procurement $133 million; relator share rules; civil penalty of $5,500-$11,000 per claim (liability, not a reward rule, not recorded); $430 million to state Medicaid from three pharmaceutical settlements; fact sheet of 10 significant recoveries. Already in the data: 6 observations and 10 qui tam cases (Merck x2, Cephalon, Amerigroup, Kyphon, SIUH x2, St. Joseph's, Bechtel/PB, CVS Caremark). Added: 3 rules and the state Medicaid figure. Not cases (no qui tam link in the release): Lester E. Cox Medical Centers $60 million, Pratt & Whitney/PCC Airfoils $53 million, the SIUH resident-count ($35.7 million) and psychiatric-bed ($1.47 million) matters. "More than $640 million" from three named settlements is a sum of named settlements, not recorded.

DOJ press release 09-1253 (19 Nov 2009) on FY2009 FCA recoveries: $2.4 billion total (second largest); more than $24 billion since 1986; nearly $2 billion from qui tam suits; $255 million to relators; relator share rules; civil penalty $5,500-$11,000 per claim (liability, not recorded); FERA 2009 amendments and HEAT task force (20 May 2009) mentioned without detail; health care $1.6 billion ("two-thirds", words, not recorded); pharmaceutical and medical device $866.7 million plus $402 million to state Medicaid; procurement $608.4 million ("a quarter", words), DoD $422 million, of which $59 million Iraq/Afghanistan war contracts; $76 million cumulative war-related; two record qui tam settlements (New York State/City $540 million, NetApp $128.7 million). Already in the data: 7 observations. Added: 3 rules, 4 observations, 2 cases. Not cases (no qui tam link in the release): Boeing (two settlements, $27 million), APL Limited $26.3 million; Aventis, Bayer, Eli Lilly and Quest/Nichols named without amounts.

DOJ press release 10-1335 (22 Nov 2010) on FY2010 FCA recoveries: $3 billion total; $2.5 billion health care (record, 83% of total); $5.4 billion since January 2009 ($4.6 billion health care); more than $27 billion since 1986; over $2.3 billion from qui tam suits; $385 million to relators; more than $18 billion qui tam recoveries and more than $2.8 billion relator awards since 1986; relators get 15-30%; pharmaceutical and medical device $1.6 billion (Pfizer $669 million FCA part of a $2.3 billion resolution, AstraZeneca $302 million, Novartis $192.7 million); Health Alliance of Greater Cincinnati/Christ Hospital $108 million; financial fraud $327.2 million (11%); Iraq/Afghanistan war contracts $10.6 million in FY2010, $137.2 million to date, $114.7 million since Jan 2009. Out of scope: FDCA criminal fines and forfeitures ($1.8 billion in FY2010, more than $3 billion since Jan 2009, 25 convictions), Pfizer criminal fines ($1.3 billion) and state Medicaid share ($331 million) of the Pfizer resolution (a single named settlement, not a case here). HEAT (20 May 2009), FERA 2009 and the ACA amendments are mentioned; FERA and ACA are already in the timeline from the statutes. Already in the data: 7 observations. Added: 2 rules and 9 observations. No cases: the named settlements are not linked to a qui tam suit in this release ("most of the cases ... were brought ... by whistleblowers" is general).

DOJ press release 11-1665 (19 Dec 2011) on FY2011 FCA recoveries: more than $3 billion total; $8.7 billion since January 2009; record $2.8 billion in qui tam cases; more than $30 billion since 1986; 28% of 25-year recoveries since January 2009; health care $2.4 billion, $6.6 billion since January 2009; more than 7,800 qui tam suits since 1986, peak of 638 in FY2011 ("300s and low 400s" earlier in the decade: words, not recorded); pharmaceutical nearly $2.2 billion ($1.76 billion federal, $421 million state Medicaid), including $900 million from eight drug manufacturers (pricing) and GlaxoSmithKline $750 million (criminal and civil, no qui tam link, not a case); non-war procurement and consumer financial fraud nearly $358 million; procurement $422 million, of which $89.3 million war-related; war-related $153.4 million and procurement $1.5 billion since January 2009. Out of scope: FDCA criminal results (21 convictions, $1.3 billion). HEAT, FERA and ACA mentioned (FERA and ACA already in the timeline). Already in the data: 6 observations. Added: 12 observations. No rules, no cases.

DOJ press release (4 Dec 2012) on FY2012 FCA recoveries: record $4.9 billion; $13.3 billion since January 2009; relator gets up to 30%; record 647 qui tam suits and $3.3 billion in whistleblower suits; health care over $3 billion, more than $9.5 billion since January 2009; housing and mortgage $1.4 billion; drugs and devices nearly $2 billion federal plus $745 million to state Medicaid; named settlements GSK $1.5 billion (part of a $3 billion global settlement), Merck $441 million (plus nearly $322 million criminal fines and more than $200 million to states), Abbott $561 million (counted in FY2013), $25 billion national mortgage servicer agreement (more than $900 million FCA), Deutsche Bank/MortgageIT $202.3 million, CitiMortgage $158.3 million, Flagstar $132.8 million, ATK $37 million, Maersk $31.9 million, Oracle $200 million: none linked to a qui tam suit or relator in this release, so not cases; procurement $427 million, $1.7 billion since January 2009; war-related $73 million; nearly 8,500 qui tam suits since 1986, nearly 2,200 since January 2009; qui tam recoveries $24.2 billion since 1986, nearly $10.5 billion since January 2009; nearly $4 billion and $439 million to whistleblowers. Out of scope: FDCA criminal results (14 convictions, $1.5 billion). Already in the data: 8 observations. Added: 1 rule, 10 observations.

DOJ press release (20 Dec 2013) on FY2013 FCA recoveries: $3.8 billion (second largest); $17 billion since January 2009 ("nearly half" since 1986, words); health care $2.6 billion, $12.1 billion since January 2009; drugs and devices $1.8 billion; state Medicaid $443 million; procurement record $890 million (also "more than $887 million" in the procurement section); relator up to 30%; 752 qui tam suits (433 in FY2009; "three to four hundred" 2000-2009, words); qui tam recoveries $2.9 billion, $13.4 billion since January 2009; whistleblower awards $345 million, $1.98 billion since January 2009; named matters Abbott $1.5 billion ($575 million federal civil, $225 million state, nearly $700 million criminal), Amgen $762 million ($598.5 million FCA), Ranbaxy $505 million ($237 million federal), Tuomey $237 million judgment, Wasserman $26.3 million (and Tampa Pathology $950,000), UTC $664 million judgment, W.W. Grainger $70 million, RPM/Tremco $61 million, Toyo Ink $45 million, Education Holdings $10 million: none linked to a qui tam suit or relator in this release, so not cases. Out of scope: FDCA criminal results (16 convictions, more than $1.3 billion). Already in the data: 8 observations. Added: 1 rule, 6 observations.

DOJ press release (20 Nov 2014) on FY2014 FCA recoveries: record $5.69 billion; $22.75 billion since January 2009 ("more than half" since 1986, words); housing and mortgage $3.1 billion (Bank of America $1.85 billion of a $16.65 billion global resolution, JPMorgan $614 million, SunTrust $428 million/$418 million, U.S. Bank $200 million), $4.65 billion since January 2009; health care $2.3 billion, $14.5 billion since January 2009; hospitals $333 million; named health care settlements J&J $1.1 billion (plus more than $600 million to states, $485 million criminal), Omnicare $116 million (plus $8.2 million to states), Community Health Systems $98.15 million, Halifax $85 million, Amedisys $150 million, cardiac trio $85 million (Boston Scientific/Guidant $30 million, King's Daughters $39 million + $2 million state, St. Joseph $16 million + $366,000 state); Hewlett-Packard $32.5 million, Boeing $23 million, BNP Paribas $80 million judgment; CA Inc. intervened whistleblower suit; relator up to 30%; more than 700 qui tam suits in FY2013 and FY2014, 30 in 1987 ("300 to 400 a year from 2000 to 2009" is an approximate description, not a count for a defined period, not recorded); qui tam recoveries nearly $3 billion; $435 million to whistleblowers; more than $2.47 billion since January 2009. Out of scope: FFETF total of more than 60 cases and more than $85 billion against financial institutions since 2009 (all remedies, not FCA). Only CA Inc. is linked to a whistleblower suit; the other named settlements are not, so they are not cases. Already in the data: 6 observations. Added: 1 rule, 7 observations, 1 case (CA Inc., pending).

DOJ press release (3 Dec 2015) on FY2015 FCA recoveries: more than $3.5 billion; $26.4 billion since January 2009; health care $1.9 billion, nearly $16.5 billion since January 2009; government contracts $1.1 billion, nearly $4 billion since January 2009; hospitals nearly $330 million; pharmaceutical $96 million; housing and mortgage $365 million, over $5 billion since January 2009; relator up to 30%; 638 qui tam suits; qui tam recoveries $2.8 billion, $19.4 billion since January 2009; whistleblower awards $597 million, $3 billion since January 2009; Yates memo on individual accountability (9 Sep 2015, not a whistleblower rule, not recorded); qui tam matters: cardiac-device suit against nearly 500 hospitals ($250 million, $216 million in FY2015), interventions against Berkeley HeartLab/BlueWave and individuals and against Dr. Qamar. Already in the data: 7 observations. Added: 1 rule, 8 observations, 3 cases.

DOJ press release (14 Dec 2016) on FY2016 FCA recoveries: more than $4.7 billion (third highest); $31.3 billion since FY2009 (yearly average nearly $4 billion, not recorded); 60% of recoveries since 1986 in the last eight years; health care $2.5 billion, $19.3 billion since January 2009 (57% of health care recoveries since 1986); drugs and devices $1.2 billion; hospitals and outpatient clinics $360 million; nursing homes more than $160 million; housing and mortgage nearly $1.7 billion (also printed as $1.6 billion), more than $7 billion since January 2009; customs $50 million; relator up to 30%; 702 qui tam suits ("13.5 new cases every week", an average, not recorded); qui tam recoveries $2.9 billion, nearly $24 billion since January 2009; whistleblower awards $519 million, more than $4 billion since January 2009. Named settlements, none linked to a qui tam suit or relator in this release (not cases): Wyeth/Pfizer $784.6 million ($413.2 million federal, $371.4 million state), Novartis $390 million ($306.9 million federal), Tenet $244.2 million (+ $123.7 million state, $145 million forfeited), Millennium Health $260 million, RehabCare/Kindred $125 million, Wells Fargo $1.2 billion, Freedom Mortgage $113 million, BP $82.6 million, L-3 EOTech $25.6 million, Education Management $52.6 million, Dr. Qamar $2 million plus $5.3 million suspended funds (linked to qui tam suits only in the FY2015 release), and ten individuals held personally liable (Hepburn $10.3 million to Scappa $250,000). DOJ press release (21 Dec 2017) on FY2017 FCA recoveries: more than $3.7 billion; more than $56 billion since 1986; health care $2.4 billion; drugs and devices over $900 million; housing and mortgage over $543 million; individuals more than $60 million (not jointly liable); 669 qui tam suits ("more than 12 new cases every week", average, not recorded); qui tam recoveries $3.4 billion; $392 million to whistleblowers. DOJ press release (21 Dec 2018) on FY2018 FCA recoveries: more than $2.8 billion; more than $59 billion since 1986; health care $2.5 billion; relator up to 30%; 645 qui tam suits ("more than 12 new cases every week", average, not recorded); qui tam recoveries over $2.1 billion; $301 million to whistleblowers; Zylon body-armour matters more than $132 million to date; increasing use of the government's dismissal authority (no numbers).
